name: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
analogy: Think of it as the cocktail party trick. Several microphones record several people talking at once, and every recording is a blend. The model works out how to unmix them back into the separate voices; here the microphones are instruments and the voices are the hidden forces that drive them.

steps.title: Collect several mixed signals
steps.description: The model takes a table where each column is a series that is a blend of hidden sources, such as the returns of several instruments over the same bars. It assumes the sources were mixed in fixed proportions.
steps.inExample: The table holds 5-minute returns of six futures: MNQ, ES, RTY (Russell 2000), ZN (ten-year note), GC (gold) and CL (crude oil), over a year.

steps.title: Centre and flatten the data
steps.description: Each series has its average removed, and then the data is rotated and scaled so that the series are uncorrelated and equally sized. This step, called whitening, leaves only a rotation to be found.
steps.inExample: After whitening, the six return series are uncorrelated, each with the same typical size.

steps.title: Look for the least bell-shaped direction
steps.description: Mixtures of independent sources tend to look more bell-shaped than the sources themselves, so the model searches for directions in which the data looks least bell-shaped. Such directions are the likely sources.
steps.inExample: One direction shows fat tails and frequent large moves, very unlike a bell shape, and is taken as the first source.

steps.title: Pull out that source
steps.description: The direction found gives a weight for each series, and combining the series with those weights produces one clean source signal. The weights show how strongly each series is tied to that source.
steps.inExample: The first source gives large weight to MNQ, ES and RTY, and small weights to ZN, GC and CL.

steps.title: Repeat for the remaining sources
steps.description: The search continues for further directions that are also unlike a bell shape and are unrelated to the ones already found. Each pass peels off another independent source, until the wanted number is reached.
steps.inExample: Three sources are kept: an equity-wide source, a bonds-and-gold source and an energy source.

steps.title: Keep the unmixing recipe
steps.description: The result is a recipe that turns the mixed series into the independent sources, and a matching recipe that blends the sources back. The recipe can be applied to any new row of the same six series.
steps.inExample: The recipe converts any set of six returns into three source readings.

steps.title: Use the sources as cleaner features
steps.description: The source signals can be used in place of the raw series: fewer inputs, and each says something distinct. Their order and sign are arbitrary, so they must be named by inspecting their weights.
steps.inExample: The three source readings replace the six raw returns as inputs to a regime classifier.

useFor.task: Pulling market-wide forces out of many instruments
useFor.example: Separating an equity-wide factor from a rates factor and an energy factor using six futures contracts.

useFor.task: Reducing the number of model inputs
useFor.example: Replacing 30 correlated indicator columns with 5 independent components before training a classifier.
Removing a component that is mostly random jitter from a set of 1-minute features.
Spotting minutes when a component takes a far larger value than it ever did in training.

avoidWhen: Your series are mostly bell-shaped; the method relies on departures from a bell shape to separate sources, so it cannot unmix them, and principal component analysis is the better choice.
You need components ranked by importance; the components come out in no particular order and with arbitrary sign, so principal component analysis, which ranks by variance, is better suited.

example.scenario: A researcher unmixes the 5-minute returns of six futures contracts into three independent sources, then reads the sources for one bar.

input.summary: One row of six returns for the same 5-minute bar, in basis points (one basis point is one hundredth of a percent).

fields.name: MNQ return
fields.meaning: The change in the micro Nasdaq future over the bar.

fields.name: ES return
fields.meaning: The change in the S&P 500 future over the bar.

fields.name: RTY return
fields.meaning: The change in the Russell 2000 future over the bar.

fields.name: ZN return
fields.meaning: The change in the ten-year note future over the bar.

fields.name: GC return
fields.meaning: The change in the gold future over the bar.

fields.name: CL return
fields.meaning: The change in the crude oil future over the bar.

output.summary: Three independent source readings, in standard deviations, and what each source is tied to.

fields.name: source 1, equity-wide
fields.meaning: A strong positive reading on the source tied mostly to MNQ, ES and RTY.

fields.name: source 2, bonds and gold
fields.value: under half a standard deviation below average
fields.meaning: A mild negative reading on the source tied to ZN and GC.

fields.name: source 3, energy
fields.value: a little over half a standard deviation above average
fields.meaning: A modest positive reading on the source tied mainly to CL.

fields.name: weight of MNQ on source 1
fields.meaning: How strongly MNQ is tied to the equity-wide source; 100 would be fully tied.

example.reading: The move is almost entirely an equity-wide one, with a small energy contribution and little from bonds or gold. Use the three readings as compact inputs to a model, but name the sources by checking their weights on each new fit, because their order and sign can flip between fits.
